label: tool-anchor-probe
_why: THE LADDER'S ANCHOR RUNG, MEASURED (user-proposed and user-ordered 2026-09-19: 'e1 is the anchor, with the in1 applied to inputs. Then, t2 output is anchor x A. Not A^2. Tier0 output is anchor / A. Same for inputs.' then 'Try measuring it in 1836-1838 first. N=10 on anchoring tools at e1 and n=10 on anchoring tools at e2.'). FINDINGS F148 is the paper case: the 1836 map does not stand on e0 in every industry - tooling's mass is on e2 (50 of its 95 levels, the only material e2 presence anywhere on the map), gated on mechanical_tools, a GAME-ERA-2 technology vanilla hands the leaders at the start, yet priced as a 1905 rung at A^2 = 4.84x its own vanilla method's output. That is tooling's +54% share of F137's anchor error and, through its output, its 369%-of-base reservation price for steel against the motor industry's 100%. Shifting the exponent's origin is a pure LEVEL shift: it moves margin, anchor error and absolute input/output, and leaves every ratio BETWEEN rungs - and therefore F97's death test - identical.

_arms.probe-tool-a1: THE USER'S OWN PROPOSAL. tooling's ladder anchored on its e1 rung (vanilla pm_pig_iron, wood 30 + iron 20 -> 60 tools, x1.2 on inputs): e0 27.3 tools / wood 56 | e1 60 / wood 36 + iron 24 | e2 132 / wood 47.3 + steel 31.5 | e3 290.4 / rubber 19.9 + steel 59.7. Base margins -27 / +7 / +57 / +130% against the canon's 25 / 83 / 169 / 294%.
_arms.probe-tool-a2: ANCHORED ON THE RUNG THE 1836 MAP ACTUALLY SITS ON (vanilla pm_steel, wood 30 + steel 20 -> 80 tools, x1.2 on inputs): e0 16.5 / wood 42.7 | e1 36.4 / wood 27.4 + iron 18.3 | e2 80 / wood 36 + steel 24 | e3 176 / rubber 15.2 + steel 45.5. Base margins -42 / -15 / +25 / +83%. The user has named unstated considerations against this arm and wants the numbers first.

_delta: ONE LEVER against the canon, and the field diff proves it: exactly TWELVE fields move in each arm - tooling's four rungs' output_qty, inputs and target_be - and the other sixteen industries are byte-identical to config/mod_config.canon-c19-in12.json, which makes them a control built into each arm. A 2.2 / B 1.5 / in0 1.2 / cost anchor x 1.9^era / ai_value 1000x3^era / divisor 0.000125 / the 10.75 defines / the 24-month bar throughout. Generated by make_ab_config's new --anchor-for flag; both tech-tree twins are byte-identical to the canon's.
_confound_named: --anchor-for moves OUTPUT and INPUT VALUE only; building_cost and ai_value stay functions of the absolute era, because the narrative era is what says 'this is a 1905 building' (10.78 rule 3) and both are separately-swept levers. The consequence is real and must be stated in the verdict: tooling's capital per unit of output moves (a1 +10% at e2, a2 +82% at e2). Over 21 months almost nothing is built (F142: the adjustment is paid in staffing, not construction), so it barely bites here - over a century it would, and this batch does not measure that.

_predictions._basis: F148's arithmetic over the emitted 1836 history at base prices, and F142/F144/F145 for how an anchor-time recipe change actually reads. Stated before the runs.
_predictions.steel_the_headline: At the emitted levels the three books ask 1,159 (canon) / 1,719 (a1) / 1,344 (a2) units of steel against a supply of 1,105, i.e. naive implied prices of 104 / 142 / 116% of base. PREDICT a1 is the WORST steel arm ever measured on this span - ceiling share above the canon's 18% and above grad-a's 43%, staffed steel levels at or below 0.75 of vanilla - and a2 sits between the canon and a1. FAILURE MODE for the whole reading: if a1's steel is NOT worse than the canon's, then reservation price, not quantity, is what sets the steel price, and F148 section 2 is the part that survives rather than section 1.
_predictions.tools_and_the_anchor: Tools output at the 1836 levels: 9,870 (canon) / 8,973 (a1) / 5,439 (a2) against vanilla's 6,400. PREDICT the tools price rises monotonically canon -> a1 -> a2 in the British and Prussian markets, and that a2 is the first arm on any book whose tools price sits ABOVE vanilla's.
_predictions.tooling_survival: Base-price margins say a1 kills tooling's e0 (-27%) and a2 kills e0 (-42%) AND e1 (-15%). Under 10.86.5 survival is read as retained staffed levels, and vanilla itself sheds. PREDICT a1 retains 60-85% of tooling e0's staffed levels and a2 under 50%, with a2's e1 also shedding - that is 45 of the world's 95 tooling levels (RUS 12, AUS 5, CHI 4 and the small holders) going underwater at the anchor, which is the obsolescence goal arriving in 1836 for countries that are behind. Whether that is wanted is a ruling, not a measurement.
_predictions.world_product: PREDICT both arms within 0.95-1.02 of the canon's. a2 removes ~4,400 units/wk of tools output from the 1836 map, which is real value added, so a2 is the more likely to fall; a1 adds input cost without adding output, so it can fall too. A fall below 0.95 in either says the anchor shift is not free at the anchor.
_predictions.engines: motor e0 is untouched in both arms, so any engine movement is the steel market acting on it - which is the mechanism F148 section 2 claims. PREDICT engine consumption FALLS in a1 (dearer steel) and is flat or better in a2. n=10 is finally enough to say so: F147 section 1c ruled n=2 insufficient for the engine market at single-digit levels, and this is the first batch sized for it.
_predictions.the_control_inside_the_arm: food, textile, furniture, glass, paper, arms, artillery, steel, motor, fertilizer, explosives, munition, automotive, synthetics, electrics and the academy have IDENTICAL recipes in both arms and in the canon. Their era-0 margins and staffing retention should match the canon's within seed noise. If they move, the difference is the market answering tooling, which is a result rather than noise - read it with good_market.mjs, not price alone.

_comparison: The canon at n=3 (setup probe-in12 of session 20260919_132049, config/mod_config.canon-c19-in12.json) is the baseline arm and does NOT need re-running; vanilla at n=2 is in the same session. Same machine, same day, same game version, same span, same dump dates, so `early_probe --also` pools them.
_watch: run 1 at ~3 min: PM_TECH_REHAUL marker, game version, this run's error window BY POSITION (parsed stamps, wrap-safe), clock advancing
the first summary set: tooling levels by rung and STAFFED levels, steel staffed levels
runs 1-10 are a1 back to back, then 11-20 are a2 - configs are NOT alternated (the 2026-09-13 ruling)
post-batch: preflight -Session, VERDICT.md, SESSION_VERDICTS row, FINDINGS
_cost: 20 runs x 1836->1838 at ~3 min each, plus 20 builds and the harvest: about 80-90 minutes.
_caveats: TWO IN-GAME YEARS IS NOT THE CENTURY. This measures what the anchor shift does to the 1836 economy - prices, steel, survival, world product. It says nothing about obsolescence, the price decline, the money printer or the hoard, all of which are decades out.
The anchor shift cannot move F97's death test by construction (it is a pure level shift), so no obsolescence claim can be made from this batch in either direction.
building_cost and ai_value do not shift with the anchor - see _confound_named. a2's tooling frontier is 82% dearer per unit of output than the canon's, which this span cannot see and a century would.
n=10 per arm is the largest short batch run on this project; it is sized for the engine and steel markets, not for world GDP, whose seed spread is wider than anything two in-game years can resolve.
Launch ONLY through tools/testbed/launch_detached.ps1 CALLED DIRECTLY from the PowerShell tool (landmine L30); the STOP file must be absent.

defaults._dump_dates_note: Identical to all five probe sessions of 2026-09-19, which is what makes the canon and vanilla arms of 20260919_132049 reusable as references.
